pages.x: Babur, descended from Timur on his father's side and from Genghis Khan on his mother's, was a prince of Ferghana who won and lost Samarkand three times. Driven south, he made Kabul his base and looked to the rich lands of India.

In April 1526 he met the sultan of Delhi, Ibrahim Lodi, at Panipat, with about 12,000 men against perhaps 100,000 and a thousand war elephants. Babur chained carts together, fired cannon and muskets from behind them and sent horse archers round the flanks. Ibrahim died on the field.

Babur wrote his own memoirs, in his Turkic language: his battles, but also gardens, fruit, wine, friends and the animals of India. He missed the melons of home. It is one of the first autobiographies by a ruler.
In 1530 his son Humayun lay dying. Babur, the story goes, walked three times around the bed, praying to give his own life for his son's. Humayun recovered, and Babur fell ill and died.

Humayun lost the new empire to the Afghan Sher Shah Suri in 1540 and spent fifteen years in exile, much of it in Persia. He won Delhi back in 1555, and died a year later after falling down the stairs of his library.

Humayun's son Akbar was 13. In 1556 his guardian, Bairam Khan, beat Hemu, the Hindu general who had taken Delhi, in a second battle at Panipat. Akbar would spread the empire across most of North India and rule for 49 years.

The Mughals ruled much of India for two centuries. They left the Taj Mahal and the Red Fort, and a blend of Persian and Indian culture that shaped the Urdu language and the food, music and painting of North India and Pakistan.
pts: Humayun lost the empire and won it back
Began two centuries of Mughal rule
